newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Thousands of Liberian refugees head home to vote.
newsitem.headline: Thousands of Liberian refugees head home to vote.

text.p: Thousands of Liberian refugees are heading home from Ivory Coast to vote, speaking of promises of cash, rice and transport from candidate Charles Taylor, the man who launched their country's civil war.

Border police at Prollo, the Ivorian checkpoint beside the Cavally River 25 km (15 miles) up a bush track from the south western town of Tabou, say 600 people crossed into Liberia in 10-man dugouts on Thursday alone.
"People have short memories. Most of the people genuinely love Taylor despite what he did to some of their families," said a Roman Catholic priest.
"Others say he is the only one who can handle the situation even if they wouldn't vote for him otherwise."
Liberians queued without baggage at the crossing for passage over the 200-metre stretch of water to a Liberian checkpoint where trucks reputedly supplied by the warlord-turned-politician waited.
Returning refugees said they had been promised a kg of rice, 1000 CFA francs (about $2) and transport to and from polling stations for Saturday's elections.
"There has been a large effort by Charles Taylor to transport people back to vote. He has spent a large amount of money on this," one relief worker said.
U.N. figures suggest as many as 667,000 Liberians, out of an estimated population of three million, now live in Ivory Coast, Guinea or Sierra Leone.

The elections are part of a peace plan brokered by Liberia's West African neighbours to end seven years of civil war that has killed well over 150,000 people. Nigerian-led West African peacekeeping troops are ensuring security.
Ivorian border police said they would close the border on Friday evening. Armed Ivorian paratroopers said there had been no trouble at the border.
Relief workers estimated that thousands had crossed to vote in the Tabou area alone -- either at the official checkpoint or clandestinely further up the river.
"A lot of people went home last week to register and stayed. Others came back and are now leaving again," one aid worker said.
The senior churchman from the local town of Harper, Archbishop Nyema Daliels, now lives in San Pedro across the border in Ivory Coast and took a gloomy view of peace prospects.
"Around here all the people know about is Charles Taylor," he said. "Our people will go back and vote for him because they are afraid of him. There will be trouble whether or not he wins."
Tabou residents said Taylor supporters drove around town in May in 4x4 vehicles covered in election posters until the Ivorian authorities stopped them.

Miriam Whale, a Harper refugee in her early 30s living at a U.N. settlelemnt north of Tabou, was keen to return home. "I just want to go back home. That is the only place I can think of now because I have been here for too many years," she said.
James Wooart, 24, an ex-fighter who declined to say for whom he fought, walked two hours to reach the crossing and said he would return to Ivory Coast on Saturday night after voting.
"I am getting rice and money from Charles Taylor," he said. But it was unclear whether he would. One woman walked to Harper and returned empty handed with tales of broken promises.
